summary:
We built the MODIS–VIIRS Fire Calendar, a web app that gives Vietnam one consistent fire record from 2003 to 2026. VIIRS detects many more small fires than MODIS, so simply joining the two records makes fires appear to jump about sevenfold in 2012, when only the sensor changed. We trained a Poisson model on the years both sensors overlap to convert MODIS-Aqua counts to the VIIRS S-NPP scale, filled S-NPP outage days with NOAA-20, and validated the model on years it never saw (2018–2021: national bias −3.7%, monthly R² 0.99).

Anyone can now compare this year with past years for any of Vietnam's 34 provinces, choose a date range, compare two provinces or periods, and download the charts and data. Using NASA MCD12Q1 and ESA WorldCover, users can separate forest fires from crop burning. A patrol priority map combines how often each 1 km cell burns with how hard it is to reach, giving forest rangers a ranked list of places to patrol, with directions.

This matters because fires in Vietnam's Northwest and Central Highlands destroy forests and livelihoods every dry season, and rangers need to know where to act first.
details:
What it does ?

The MODIS–VIIRS Fire Calendar turns two generations of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent, easy-to-read fire record for Vietnam from 2003 to 2026, and turns that record into action for forest rangers.

 

• Harmonized fire calendar: monthly hotspot counts for every one of Vietnam's 34 provinces (boundaries after the July 2025 merger), all on the VIIRS S-NPP scale, so 2005 can be compared fairly with 2025.

• Interactive map: a 3D globe that flies into Vietnam; Day / Month / Quarter / Year views; a "heat glow" view and a 1 km grid view; in Day view, every real fire point with its time, satellite and fire radiative power.

• Explore & Compare: pick a province, a date range and a land cover type, or compare two of them (another province, another period, or forest vs. cropland). The tool shows summary cards, a time-series chart and a fire calendar, and everything can be downloaded as CSV or PNG.

• Year × Month calendar, before/after harmonization charts, and a custom region tool (any circle plus date range) with CSV export.

• Land cover filter: All / Forest / Cropland / Other, applied at once to the map, province ranking, charts and patrol map.

• Patrol priority map: for each province and month, every 1 km cell that burned in 2012–2025 is ranked High / Medium / Low. Tapping a cell shows how many years it burned, the distance to the nearest vehicle road, the slope and the land cover, plus a one-tap Google Maps route.

 

How it works ?

1. Data cleaning: about 2.15 million MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) detections from NASA FIRMS (archive and near-real-time). We removed volcanoes, static industrial sources, offshore points, low-confidence detections and cells that burn almost all year, leaving about 1.9 million fire points. All dates were converted from UTC to Vietnam local time.

2. Harmonization: a Poisson generalized linear model on a 0.25° monthly grid predicts the S-NPP count from the MODIS-Aqua count, whether MODIS saw any fire, the MODIS count in neighbouring cells, and a per-cell effect. It was trained on 2012–2017 and tested on 2018–2021, which it never saw: national bias −3.7%, rank correlation 0.96 between predicted and observed monthly calendars, national monthly R² 0.99. Leave-one-year-out cross-validation gives a 90% uncertainty range of about −5% to +6% on yearly totals, which the app shows as a confidence band.

3. Record assembly: modeled MODIS-Aqua values for 2003 to January 2012, observed S-NPP from February 2012. S-NPP outage passes are filled with NOAA-20, which matches S-NPP almost exactly (factor 1.006), and NOAA-20 continues the record after S-NPP ended in November 2026.

4. Land cover: each 1 km cell is labelled with ESA WorldCover 2021 (10 m) and checked against NASA MCD12Q1 for every year from 2001 to 2023. Cells where the two disagree are marked "uncertain", and cells that MODIS shows changing (for example, forest that became farmland) use the label of the fire year.

5. Patrol priority: distance to the nearest vehicle road from OpenStreetMap and mean slope from NASADEM (Google Earth Engine). High priority means a cell burned in at least 7 of 14 years and is hard to reach; Medium means at least 4 of 14 years; Low means 1–3 years. We checked the accessibility rating against satellite imagery at 10 real fire locations.

 

Benefits and intended impact

• Forest rangers see where fire keeps coming back and is hardest to reach, so a small team can plan patrols and watchtowers before the dry season peaks.

• Provincial agencies, researchers and journalists get a fair 20-year baseline: is this season really worse, or did only the sensor change?

• Separating forest fires from crop burning helps forestry focus on forests and helps agriculture and air-quality agencies track field burning. In March 2026, for example, about 52% of hotspots nationwide were on forest land and 22% on cropland, while in the Mekong Delta about 90% were on cropland.

 

How it is creative ?

We went beyond a corrected chart: the same harmonized data drives a patrol plan with directions, a land-cover lens that tells forest fire from field burning, and a compare tool that lets non-experts ask their own questions. The app works on phones (bottom-sheet panel, pinch to zoom, tap for details), is bilingual (Vietnamese and English), and has a colorblind-friendly palette.

 

Factors we considered

Different sensor sensitivity and overpass times; satellite outages and the end of S-NPP; UTC vs. local dates; the July 2025 province merger; low data reliability in small provinces (flagged in the data); honest uncertainty instead of a single number; static fire sources; and limits of land-cover maps (tree plantations count as tree cover, and burned upland fields in the Northwest often appear as shrub or grassland).

 

Tools and technologies

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, GeoPandas, Shapely, PyArrow, Matplotlib, tifffile) in Google Colab and locally; Google Earth Engine for slope and land cover; OpenStreetMap (Geofabrik) for roads; a static web app in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with D3.js and TopoJSON, with Esri World Imagery as the basemap; GitHub with GitHub Actions for data checks; hosted on Vercel.

Source code : https://github.com/1nguyen1/vietnam-fire-map-final.git 

Next steps

Daily automatic updates from FIRMS near-real-time data, early alerts for ranger stations, and extending the calendar to neighbouring Mekong countries.
